parse.title: How Url::parse() works
parse.description: Reads a URL and splits it into its parts.

slides.caption: Url::parse() follows the WHATWG URL standard, the same rules a browser uses.
The scheme comes before ://. It says how to fetch the resource.
The host is the server name. It is lowercased and checked.
The path is the part from the first / up to ? or #.
The query comes after ? and the fragment after #. The getters return them without those marks.
url.scheme(), host_str(), path(), query() and fragment() return these parts. A relative URL like "/a/b" alone is an error: use join() for those.

note.text: result: scheme https, host example.com, path /a/b, query x=1, fragment top

join.title: How Url::join() works
join.description: Resolves a relative link against a base URL, like a browser does.

l0.text: "c": relative to the folder of the base, /a/

l2.text: "/c": starts with /, relative to the host

slides.caption: join() treats its argument like a link inside the page at base.
The last segment of the base, "b", is the "file"; "c" replaces it.
A link starting with / replaces the whole path.
So "/c" becomes https://example.com/c. "../c" would go one folder up, and a full URL would replace everything.
If base ends with a slash (…/a/b/), "c" gives …/a/b/c. That trailing slash is a common surprise.

query-pairs.title: How Url::query_pairs() works
query-pairs.description: Splits the query into decoded (key, value) pairs.

slides.caption: query_pairs() splits the query at & into pairs, and each pair at = into a key and a value.
The first pair is x=1: key "x", value "1".
The second pair is y=two. Escapes are decoded: %20 or + would become a space.
Values are strings (Cow<str>): parse "1" yourself to get a number. query_pairs_mut() builds a query with the right escaping.

path-segments.title: How Url::path_segments() works
path-segments.description: Splits the path into its pieces between slashes.

slides.caption: path_segments() splits the path at every /. The leading / is skipped.
Third: "c". A trailing slash (/a/b/c/) would add an empty segment "".
path_segments() returns Option: None for URLs like mailto:x@y.com that cannot have a path with slashes.

scheme.title: How Url::scheme works
scheme.description: The scheme of the URL, lowercase, without "://".

note.text: every part has its own method

slides.caption: A parsed Url knows where each part starts: scheme, user, host, port, path, query and fragment.
host_str, port, path, query and fragment read the other parts.

host-str.title: How Url::host_str works
host-str.description: The host as text, if the URL has one.

slides.caption: IPv6 hosts come back in brackets.
host() returns a typed Host enum.

port.title: How Url::port works
port.description: The port written in the URL; None if it is absent or the default for the scheme.

slides.caption: Default ports (443 for https) are not stored.

port-or-known-default.title: How Url::port_or_known_default works
port-or-known-default.description: The port, falling back to the scheme's default (80, 443...).

slides.caption: None for schemes without a known default.

path.title: How Url::path works
path.description: The path, always starting with "/" for http-like URLs.

slides.caption: Percent-encoded as it appears in the URL.
From the first / after the host.

query.title: How Url::query works
query.description: The query string after "?", without the "?".

slides.caption: Browsers never send it to the server.

username.title: How Url::username works
username.description: The user name in the URL, or "" if none.

slides.caption: Avoid putting real passwords in URLs.

as-str.title: How Url::as_str works
as-str.description: The whole URL as a normalized string.

slides.caption: Parsing lowercases scheme and host and adds the root path.

domain.title: How Url::domain works
domain.description: The host if it is a domain name; None for IP addresses.

origin.title: How Url::origin works
origin.description: Scheme + host + port: what browsers use for the same-origin policy.

slides.caption: Two URLs with the same origin may share cookies and storage.

make-relative.title: How Url::make_relative works
make-relative.description: A relative reference from this URL to another one.

slides.caption: None if the scheme or host differ.
Characters that need it are percent-encoded.

set-query.title: How Url::set_query works
set-query.description: Replaces (or removes, with None) the query string.

slides.caption: You must encode the text yourself; query_pairs_mut does it for you.

query-pairs-mut.title: How Url::query_pairs_mut works
query-pairs-mut.description: Adds or rewrites key=value pairs, encoding them correctly.

slides.caption: Spaces become +, and & or = inside values are percent-encoded, so the query stays valid.
clear() first to replace all pairs.

set-host.title: How Url::set_host works
set-host.description: Replaces the host; Err if the new host is invalid.

slides.caption: Some URLs (like mailto:) cannot have a host.
Setting the scheme's default port removes it from the text.
Err(()) for URLs that cannot have a port.

set-scheme.title: How Url::set_scheme works
set-scheme.description: Changes the scheme, if the change is allowed.

slides.caption: Switching between "special" (http) and other schemes is refused.

path-segments-mut.title: How Url::path_segments_mut works
path-segments-mut.description: Edits the path segment by segment, encoding each one.

slides.caption: Each push is one segment: a "/" inside is encoded.
Err for URLs without a hierarchical path.

from-file-path.title: How Url::from_file_path works
from-file-path.description: Turns an absolute file path into a file:// URL.

host.title: How Url::host works
host.description: The host as a typed value: Domain, Ipv4 or Ipv6.

has-host.title: How Url::has_host works
has-host.description: true if the URL has a host part.

slides.caption: mailto:, data: and similar URLs have no host.

cannot-be-a-base.title: How Url::cannot_be_a_base works
cannot-be-a-base.description: true for URLs that cannot have relative URLs joined onto them.
